title: Proof of Reserves: What It Is and How It's Verified
summary: Proof of reserves shows assets cover customer balances at one moment. Learn what it proves, what it misses, and the four steps to verify it for an auditor.
body_markdown:
On October 15, 2021, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) ordered Tether to pay a[$41 million penalty](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8450-21) for misrepresenting its dollar backing. The order also found that Tether picked the date of its accountant's reserve review in advance, and that Bitfinex transferred over $382 million to Tether's bank account ahead of it. A single snapshot can look clean on a chosen day.


Stablecoin issuers, custodians, and exchanges publish proof of reserves reports to show that customer balances are backed by real assets. Regulators in the US, EU, and UK now require an independent check of those reports, so how you verify reserves determines whether the report passes the independent check.


Verification is what turns a proof of reserves into a defensible disclosure. Without it, a token holder cannot tell whether their balance is backed, a regulator cannot tell whether the issuer is solvent, and the issuer cannot show an auditor where the number came from.


Verifying a proof of reserves starts with understanding what it proves, what it misses, and the four-step workflow that produces the evidence. Two foundations support it all: the check your regulator requires and a reproducible ledger.


### What is a proof of reserves?


A proof of reserves is a report showing an institution holds enough assets to cover what it owes customers at a specific moment. The report covers two halves:


1


**The asset half:** what the institution holds in bank accounts, custodian accounts, and on-chain wallets.


2


**The liability half:** the balances it owes customers, recorded in its core ledger.


If the assets equal or exceed the liabilities, the reserves are covered.


The asset half is proven with outside evidence. Bank and custodian statements confirm the balance in each account, and signed messages from on-chain wallets confirm the institution controls those wallets. The report shows the assets exist at that moment, but it does not prove exclusive ownership.


The liability half is harder to prove. Liabilities are promises to each customer, and they exist only as ledger entries. No outside party can confirm the total is complete, which is why[warehousing promises](https://www.formance.com/blog/engineering/warehousing-promises) is the practice the whole exercise depends on.


Regulators can only test liabilities that a ledger can reproduce at the cutoff. Formance is an open-source,[programmable core ledger](https://www.formance.com/modules/ledger) that unifies fiat and digital assets with regulatory-grade traceability and keeps an immutable, queryable record of every entry.


Verification catches the liabilities a snapshot alone would hide. A clean-looking total means nothing without a repeatable workflow behind it.


### What a proof of reserves proves and what it misses


A proof of reserves proves coverage at one moment and includes each customer in the total. The proof of reserves misses liabilities that were never recorded, and it doesn't show whether assets are free of claims or remain in place.


#### Proves the coverage at one moment


At the cutoff moment, the reserves shown are equal to or greater than the customer balances on record.


The liability total comes from the ledger, the asset total comes from banks and custodians, and both are compared at the same timestamp.


The coverage claim applies only to the cutoff instant, so a match at that timestamp says nothing about whether reserves still cover balances later.


#### Proves each customer is included in the total


A customer can verify that their balance was included in the published total without seeing anyone else's balance.


The report uses a summation Merkle tree, a data structure where each leaf holds one customer's balance and each level above it holds the sum of the leaves below. The top of the tree, called the root, stands for the total.


Each customer gets a path from their leaf up to the root. Matching that path against the published root shows their balance was included at the cutoff. The tree proves each customer is included, but doesn't prove the total itself is complete.


#### Misses the liabilities that were never recorded


The snapshot proves nothing about balances the issuer never wrote down, or wrote down falsely.


If an operator credits fake accounts and trades them against real customers, the ledger still adds up cleanly because the fraud lives inside the entries themselves.


A Merkle root built over a fake extract only commits to the numbers the operator chose to include.


#### Misses whether assets are free of claims, and whether they stay put


The report says nothing about whether the assets shown were pledged, lent, or moved after the cutoff. A bank confirmation shows a balance, and a signed wallet message shows control of a key at that moment.


Neither the bank confirmation nor the signed wallet message reveals whether the balance is pledged as collateral, subject to a repo, or promised to another counterparty.


No point-in-time report tells you whether those same assets were wired out, lent, or encumbered the moment after the cutoff.


### The proof-of-reserves check each regulator requires


Your regulator decides which proof-of-reserves check you need: a monthly examination under US rules, a six-month audit for some EU issuers, or an annual reasonable assurance review under UK rules. Agreed-upon procedures meet none of them, because they report findings without giving assurance.


In the US,[Section 4(a)(3)(A)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/html/PLAW-119publ27.htm) of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins[(GENIUS) Act](https://www.formance.com/glossary/genius-act) requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to have a registered public accounting firm examine their month-end reserve report every month.


The Act takes effect on[January 18, 2027](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/10/2026-06974/genius-act-requirements-and-standards-for-fdic-supervised-permitted-payment-stablecoin-issuers-and) , or 120 days after the primary federal regulators issue final rules, if that comes first.


In the EU,[Article 36(9)](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-36-obligation-have-reserve-assets) of the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation[(MiCA)](https://www.formance.com/glossary/mica-act) requires asset-referenced token issuers to mandate an independent reserve audit every six months.[Article 58(1)](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-58-specific-additional-obligations) applies the same audit to e-money institutions issuing significant e-money tokens, starting from the date the token is classified as significant.


Non-significant e-money tokens have no six-month audit by default.[Article 54](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-54-investment-funds-received) governs how they hold their funds, and under Article 58(2) the home regulator can impose the Article 36 requirements.


In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA)[Policy Statement PS26/10](https://www.fca.org.uk/publication/policy/ps26-10.pdf) requires qualifying stablecoin issuers to have their published 1:1 backing statements independently reviewed at least every 12 months.


These rules, and[chapter 16 of the FCA’s](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/cass16/cass16s2?date=25-10-2027&timeline=true) Client Assets Sourcebook, come into force on October 25, 2027.


### How proof of reserves is verified in four steps


Verification is a four-step workflow that produces the evidence behind a proof of reserves. The steps are: take the liability snapshot from the core ledger, take the asset snapshot and apply eligibility tests, reconcile both snapshots at the cutoff, and publish the artifacts an engagement can test.


#### Step 1: Take the liability snapshot from the core ledger


The liability snapshot is the total of every customer balance at one cutoff, extracted from the core ledger as a single reproducible query. The query sums every @customers:*:available balance at the cutoff timestamp, and that sum is the snapshot.


A settled deposit written in[Numscript](https://www.formance.com/platform/numscript) shows what one of those balances looks like. A $4,000,000 wire lands and clears, moving from the settled omnibus boundary @platform:banks:primary:omnibus:settled to customer 88213's available balance at @customers:88213:available.


```text
// SETTLED_DEPOSIT
// Event: credit customer 88213 after a USD 4,000,000 wire settles


send   [USD/2 400000000]   (
source   =   @platform:banks:primary:omnibus:settled   allowing   unbounded   overdraft
destination   =   @customers:88213:available
)


set_tx_meta  (  "event_type"  ,   "settled_deposit"  )
set_tx_meta  (  "transfer_id"  ,   "wire88213"  )


```


For the snapshot to hold up months later, the query must return the same totals every time it runs.


#### Step 2: Take the asset snapshot and apply eligibility tests


The asset snapshot pulls balances from every bank, custodian, and on-chain wallet at the same cutoff timestamp. Count an asset as a reserve only when it passes the eligibility tests of owned, unencumbered, settled, and available at that cutoff.


Each eligibility test has a common way it fails:


•


**Owned:** the asset fails this test when operating cash, or funds from unclear sources, sits in the reserve account and gets counted as customer backing.


•


**Unencumbered:** the asset fails this test when it has been lent out or pledged as collateral.


•


**Settled:** the asset fails this test when an on-chain confirmation is treated as[final settlement](https://www.formance.com/glossary/settlement-finality) , or when the bank has not yet credited an incoming wire.


•


**Available:** the asset fails this test when custody evidence proves control of a key without proving the asset is free to use.


Anything that clears all four tests belongs in the asset total. Exclude or flag anything that fails one of the eligibility tests before comparing the total against the liability snapshot.


#### Step 3: Reconcile both snapshots at the cutoff


Cutoff reconciliation gates both snapshots, and any unreconciled input invalidates the proof. When an internal ledger and its partner bank are never reconciled to the same moment, every customer balance can still pass a[Merkle inclusion check](https://gateway-docs.unruggable.com/fundamentals/what-is-an-inclusion-proof) while the aggregate falls short of the bank's actual position.


One input to catch every month is the on-chain balance that is confirmed at the cutoff but not yet economically settled, because[on-chain confirmation is not settlement](https://www.formance.com/blog/financial-operations/on-chain-confirmation-is-not-settlement) .


Run balance-level checks against banks and custodians first, then transaction-level checks on the exceptions.


#### Step 4: Publish the proof of reserves report an auditor can test


The report includes a dated cutoff extract, the versioned inclusion rules that produced it, and the reconciliation result.


List every leaf, including zero-balance accounts, so an auditor can tell a missing zero from a missing liability. Keep negative balances as their own exceptions rather than netting them against positives.


The extract has to be reproducible on demand, either persisted and versioned or regenerated by the pinned bi-temporal query from Step 1.


Stablecoin issuers publish to a public disclosure page, while custodians and e-money institutions deliver directly to the auditor and regulator under a restricted-use engagement.


### How to make your proof of reserves reproducible


The second requirement for verifying a proof of reserves is a ledger that can regenerate the snapshot on demand. The ledger determines whether you can reproduce the totals you disclose months later under examination.


Start by storing the liability snapshot from Step 1 so the auditor can rerun it. Either save it as a versioned file, or leave it as a query the ledger will always answer the same way.


A ledger built for this has three properties:


1


**Immutable history:** Entries are hash-chained, so no one can quietly edit a past entry after the cutoff.


2


**Point-in-time queries:** The ledger can answer "what was every balance at this timestamp?" using bi-temporal queries, so the cutoff snapshot can be regenerated months later.


3


**Versioned inclusion rules:** The rules that decide which accounts count toward the total are saved with each snapshot, so the auditor can see exactly which accounts were counted.


Without these properties, you can't reproduce the snapshot. A script that reads today's balances and subtracts recent activity won't work, because the totals will drift every time it runs.
